fixes.explanation: That's the list, baker. Genesis 13:2 says Abram had become extremely wealthy in livestock and silver and gold. Three things, and he's loaded with every one. I started out with a 25 cent price sticker on me, so I'm taking notes.

Land and vineyards would be a nice portfolio, but that's not what the verse says. Genesis 13:2 says Abram had become extremely wealthy in livestock and silver and gold. Land and vineyards didn't make that list. Look at it again, baker, and you'll spot what did.

True! Genesis 13:4 says Abram called on the name of the LORD there, at the site where he had built the altar. He had built that altar earlier, between Bethel and Ai (Genesis 12:8). Now he's back at the same spot, calling on the LORD again. I love that.

Not quite, friend. The text says Abram came to the site where he had built the altar, and there he called on the name of the LORD (Genesis 13:4). So the statement on the card is true. Abram was there calling on the LORD, and the verse says so plainly.

Look at what the text says, baker. It says the land was unable to support both of them while they stayed together, for they had so many possessions (Genesis 13:6). So the statement is false. Staying together was the trouble, and the verse says they were unable to coexist.

False is right! Genesis 13:6 says the land was unable to support both of them while they stayed together, for they had so many possessions. They were unable to coexist. Two men with that much stuff, and together it just didn't work.

Yes, Lot. Genesis 13:7 says there was discord between the herdsmen of Abram and the herdsmen of Lot. Lot is the one who was traveling with Abram (Genesis 13:5). I think the herdsmen were stuck in the middle of this one.

Pharaoh, the ruler of Egypt (Genesis 12:15), belongs to the last chapter, not this fight. Abram has already gone up out of Egypt (Genesis 13:1). The discord is between the herdsmen of Abram and the herdsmen of Lot (Genesis 13:7). This one stays in the traveling group.

Kinsmen! Abram says it plainly: "After all, we are kinsmen." (Genesis 13:8) He wants no contention between him and Lot, or between their herdsmen. I think that's wise. Some arguments cost way more than they're worth.

To the right! Abram says, "If you go to the left, I will go to the right; if you go to the right, I will go to the left." (Genesis 13:9) He offers to take the opposite direction from whatever Lot picks. Lot gets to choose first. That's a generous offer.

Dry and rocky is the opposite of what he sees, baker. The text says the whole plain of the Jordan, all the way to Zoar, was well watered (Genesis 13:10). It even compares it to the garden of the LORD and the land of Egypt. Nobody calls dust and rocks a garden.

Forest? Nice try, friend, but I don't see one tree in this verse. What Lot sees is that the whole plain of the Jordan was well watered (Genesis 13:10). The plain gets compared to the garden of the LORD and the land of Egypt, but trees never come up.

EAST! Genesis 13:11 says Lot chose the whole plain of the Jordan for himself and set out toward the east. The WHOLE plain, baker. He didn't pick a corner, he picked it all. Then the verse says Abram and Lot parted company.

An altar to the LORD, yes! Genesis 13:18 says Abram built it at Hebron, near the Oaks of Mamre. He had built an altar earlier between Bethel and Ai (Genesis 12:8). Now there's a new one by his new home.

A well would be handy with all those herds, baker, but that's not what the text says. Abram built an altar to the LORD (Genesis 13:18). The earlier altar was between Bethel and Ai (Genesis 13:3-4). A well never comes up at Hebron.
